title: Reasoning models and chain of thought
matchup: Wei et al. (2022), OpenAI o1 (2024) and DeepSeek-R1 (2025) vs Schmidhuber's "On Learning to Think" (2015)
question: Does the 2015 controller-and-world-model proposal establish the priority Schmidhuber claims for chain-of-thought and reinforcement-learned reasoning?

usual_credit.summary: Chain-of-thought prompting is usually credited to Wei et al. (2022), who showed that large language models solve arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic problems better when they write out intermediate reasoning steps, with closely related work on scratchpads by Nye et al. (2021). Models trained with reinforcement learning to produce a long chain of thought before answering were introduced by OpenAI with o1 in September 2024, and DeepSeek reported in January 2025 that reasoning abilities of language models can be incentivized through pure reinforcement learning without human-labeled reasoning examples.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber argues that his 2015 On Learning to Think report anticipated reinforcement-learned reasoning by training a controller to query a recurrent world model and use its answers for planning. He now calls the controller a prompt engineer and the interaction an adaptive chain of thought, while acknowledging that its prompts are internal vectors rather than necessarily natural-language text. He links the 2018 One Big Net for Everything proposal to combining controller and model through distillation, and says DeepSeek-R1 uses elements of these ideas. His priority claim concerns the control-and-query principle, rather than an earlier language model with DeepSeek-R1's reported results.

response.summary: Wei and colleagues' chain-of-thought paper studies intermediate reasoning written by a language model, whereas the 2015 report studies a controller exchanging activations with a fixed recurrent world model. DeepSeek-R1 studies reinforcement learning for language-model reasoning, including training without human-labelled reasoning examples. Neither paper cites On Learning to Think. The linked sources do not include a direct reply from those authors or OpenAI, so the architectural and training differences provide a comparison rather than evidence that the later authors accepted or rejected Schmidhuber's proposed connection.

agreed_facts: Schmidhuber's report "On Learning to Think" was posted to arXiv on 30 November 2015, and its abstract says the system learns to query its model for abstract reasoning and planning, "essentially 'learning to think'".
Wei et al. posted "Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models" on arXiv on 28 January 2022, and the DeepSeek-R1 report appeared on 22 January 2025.
OpenAI introduced o1 on 12 September 2024 as a model trained with reinforcement learning that produces a long internal chain of thought before answering.
Neither the chain-of-thought paper nor the DeepSeek-R1 report lists "On Learning to Think" in its references.
In the 2015 report the controller's connections are trained by reinforcement learning while the connections of the world model stay fixed.
crux: The sources differ on whether a reinforcement learning controller that queries a recurrent world model, as described in 2015, is the same idea as a language model that writes out reasoning steps in text, or only a loosely related precursor. They also differ on whether the authors of the 2022 to 2025 work knew of the 2015 report.

card.headline: Chain-of-thought reasoning models
card.question: Did Schmidhuber's 2015 report On Learning to Think anticipate chain-of-thought reasoning in language models?
card.claim: He says his 2015 controller, trained by reinforcement learning to query a world model for planning, is what is now called chain of thought.
card.pushback: No reply from the later authors is on record, and his controller passes internal vectors to a fixed model rather than writing out text.
card.crux: The question is whether a controller querying a world model is the same idea as a language model writing out its reasoning.
